Creative Readings: Essays on Seminal Analytic Works. Thomas H. Ogden. London and New York: Routledge, 2012. 201 pp.

Uta Gosmann

Uta Gosmann

Uta Gosmann  

Sometimes you have the good fortune of becoming a psychoanalyst by learning directly and in person from a great analyst. Even if that great analyst has died, you can still learn from him by going to his writings, where you can intimately experience his thinking and practice. Some analysts would even argue that by immersing yourself in analysts' written legacies, you can know their work better than they knew it themselves. For this to happen, you need to become a creative reader and do what Thomas Ogden models in Creative Readings: Essays on Seminal Analytic Works. A creative reader does with texts what a psychoanalyst does with patients: he senses and gradually comes to know something about the other that has eluded that person. He also allows himself to be “read by the writing” (p. 2)—just as the analyst allows himself to be transformed by a patient—and by giving himself over to the experience of reading gains access to a new part of himself.

In Creative Readings, Ogden evokes the experience of reading and being read by texts that have been constitutive in his own evolution as a psychoanalyst. He chooses Freud's “Mourning and Melancholia” (1917), Susan Isaacs's “The Nature and Function of Phantasy” (1943), W. R. D. Fairbairn's “Schizoid Factors in the Personality” (1940) and “Endopsychic Structure Considered in Terms of Object-Relationships” (1944)

Marcus Silverman

Marcus Silverman

Marcus Silverman  

It seems that each year brings a smattering of new books that are powerfully critical of the psychoanalytic movement. There is, then, something eminently refreshing about a straightforward book like The Letters of Sigmund Freud and Otto Rank: Inside Psychoanalysis. It contains 250 letters dating from 1906 to 1925, organized chronologically. They paint a vivid portrait of this father and son couple: their professional practices, friendships, preferences, rivalries; of administrative matters—Rank was the first secretary of Freud's Viennese Psychoanalytic Society and co-editor and publisher of both Imago and Zeitschrift

This paper describes the novel work of the Philadelphia Consultation Center, a Medicaid funded clinic that works with patients in a modern psychoanalytically-informed style. The clinic is inspired by the precedent established by Freud that psychoanalytic treatment should never be withheld from a person for lack of funds. The author also highlights the unique array of challenges inherent in rapidly training early-career clinicians to do psychoanalytic work when they themselves have never been exposed to these principles. Out of this need, a “crash course in Spotnitz” has been developed by the author in order to shape the therapeutic stances of complete beginners to psychoanalysis.

René Magritte and the Denial of Meaning

Marcus Silverman MA

Marcus Silverman

16 W. 10 St.
NY, NY 10011
Phone: (347) 807-5870
Email: msilverman@gmail.com

Marcus Silverman   Advanced candidate at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. His paper, “Homesickness: Rene Magritte and the Denial of Meaning in Words and Images,” upon which the paper in the journal is based, was awarded the NAAP Gradiva Award for Best Student Paper in 2011. Prior, he earned a M.A. in Psychoanalysis from the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis and a B.A. in Philosophy from Sarah Lawrence College in Bronxville, New York. He lives and works in New York City.

René Magritte presented himself as an uncomplicated man. A prolific painter who is regarded as a principal member of the Surrealist movement, his work is celebrated for its technical form and its ability to meld the commonplace with the strange and the uncanny. This paper examines what many scholars and psychoanalysts disregard about Magritte's estimations of himself: that he was in fact a deeply complex man, and that his work reinforces these assumptions, particularly the paintings that depict his mother, who drowned in the Sambre River when he was a young boy. This paper utilizes his paintings as a set of data which illustrate the use of defense mechanisms, namely intellectualization, reaction-formations and dissociation. His paintings simultaneously address and recoil from past trauma by revealing a self-conscious landscape of widespread denial of any authentic meaning in both words and images.

In many long-term analyses there comes a time when the character is revealed, the conflicts are clear, the self-understanding is significant, and the repetitions are predictable. Barbara D'Amato   Licensed psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City and in Brooklyn, NY. She is a member of the faculty of the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis and the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS), where she is a training analyst, supervisor, and Director of the CMPS Extension Division. She lectures and writes on the topic of dreaming. Her papers include “Emotional Communication: Resolving a Resistance to Feeling Hate” and “Mary Shelley's Frankenstein: An Orphaned Author's Dream and Journey Toward Integration,” exploring the connection between authors' dreams and their literary characters. She has been an educator for more than thirty years and was formerly a Special Education Teacher in the New York City school system and Curriculum and Staff Developer at the Studio School.

This paper addresses the theory and practical application of emotional education within the treatment setting and the psychoanalytic classroom. Key to this issue is the successful resolution of resistances to progressive communication. The author traces the development of seemingly intractable negative resistances within a psychoanalytic classroom and demonstrates how these were resolved through the use of symbolic emotional communications by the instructor. The ability to feel facilitated the students' thinking. Putting all thoughts and feelings into words leads to psychic change, maturation, and cure of the patient. That is true for the psychoanalytic session, but it also works for the classroom. Emotional education teaches students to learn emotionally and didactically. Techniques for the resolution of resistances in the classroom are discussed and various case material is presented.

Tayloe Denton   Doctoral candidate at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, where she is an advisor to master's-degree students and serves on the admissions committee. She practices at The Therapy Center in Brookline, MA.

This paper explores the impact of the analyst's pregnancy on the life of the patient as well as reasons for a lack of balanced reporting on the topic. The case studies section examines and discusses cases that have been reported in the literature with a focus on patients who became pregnant or impregnated someone (the majority of which resulted in abortions) around the time of the analyst's pregnancy. These occurrences are discussed as they relate to the emergence of a triadic relationship in the treatment.

Adrian Jarreau   Practices psychoanalysis in Seattle. He is a graduate of Northwestern Psychoanalytic Society, where he is on the faculty and serves on the board of directors as treasurer and on the education committee as chair of admissions.

This paper discusses one of the oldest techniques in the practice of psychoanalysis and perhaps one of the least considered. Freud called it “evenly suspended attention.” It is attention devoid of memory and desire. Access to the unconscious mind is central to this approach and entails techniques of preventing the conscious mind from interfering in defensive ways. The emotional response of the analyst is also critical because it is from this that intuition emerges. Clinical vignettes illustrate what it means to listen with the unconscious mind and how it impacts the analytic process.

Elliot Zeisel   Graduate of the Philadelphia School of Psychoanalysis and a licensed and certified psychoanalyst. Dr. Zeisel is a Distinguished Fellow of the American Group Psychotherapy Association and serves as the Vice-Chair of the AGP A Foundation Board. He is a founder of the Center for Group Studies in New York City. Dr. Zeisel is also a faculty member and training analyst at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and is the Director of the institute's Group Department. He is a member of the Israeli Institute of Group Analysis. He has lectured on various aspects of analytic group therapy both nationally and abroad. Dr. Zeisel maintains a private practice for individual and group treatment in New York City and Austin, Texas.

This paper explores the importance and impact of the analytic group leader's emotional availability on group dynamics. The case studies brought forward by the author demonstrate that emotional learning and the meeting of maturational needs happen as a direct consequence of therapeutic responses to patients' feeling states. The complex social and emotional environment of a psychoanalytic group becomes therapeutic when the leader assumes the role of custodian of the group's culture. If the leader cultivates one's own emotional availability and receptivity, he educates his patients to do the same for themselves and others.

Patricia Bratt   Psychoanalyst practicing in Livingston, NJ and NYC, is a Director of the Academy of Clinical and Applied Psychoanalysis (ACAP) in Livingston, NJ, its Trauma and Resilience Programs, and Applied Psychoanalysis Division. She has written, spoken widely, and appeared as a guest expert on radio and TV about her work with children, families, and couples. Dr. Bratt's work in Applied Psychoanalysis has included staff development seminars and professional presentations for groups such as the Division of Youth and Family Services, the Child Life Specialists Association, NJ Crisis Negotiators Association, Jewish Family Services, and the International Neuropsychoanalytic Society. She is faculty and training supervisor at several psychoanalytic institutes, and has been graduate faculty at Drew University, Centenary College, and Union College. Her publications include, “The Impact of Strategic Emotional Communication on Memory & Identity Development,” “Nurturing Emotionally Resilient Children,” and “Loneliness, Longing and Love: Why Some People Never Find the Love They Need.”

This paper discusses the role of creativity and artistry within the psychoanalytic frame. The author investigates the inherent tension between flexibility and limitation when working within a modern psychoanalytic theory of technique. The author addresses herself to the structure and spontaneity required of the analyst when she is working toward an emotionally collaborative relationship with the patient. In particular, this article highlights the treatment technique of “consulting the patient” as a prime example of both creative innovation and therapeutic rigor.
